Arizona Grocery Co. v. Atchison, 284 U.S. 370, 388 (1932). Translated into 
modern terminology, ratemaking is an adjudication as a precondition to an 
integrated rulemaking. Licensing is similar: it typically involves an 
adjudication of an applicant’s qualifications for the purpose of determining 
whether it is in the pubfic interest to grant the appficant governmental 
permission to engage in some future activity. And when the licensing scheme 
is designed to allocate a limited resource (such as the radio spectrum), the 
agency may have to consider the comparative interests of multiple applicants. 
The APA deals with these dual character functions by forcing each into a single 
statutory classification: (1) ratemaking is rulemaking, see 5 U.S.C. § 551(4); 
and (2) hcensingis adjudication, id. § 551(6).
2. 
The Purpose of Classification. As Londoner and Bi-Metallic 
demonstrate, determining whether government action is judicial or legislative 
is necessary to determine what process is due. Similarly, the classification of 
agency action as adjudication or rulemaking under the APA primarily serves 
the goal of determining the apphcable procedural requirements. At the time of 
the APA’s adoption, formal hearings were used in both ratemaking and 
hcensing. The ICC, however, was engaged in efforts to reform its hearing 
procedures to make them less formal and more efficient. Although the APA 
predominately was designed to operate trans-substantively, a desire to aid the 
ICC’s reform efforts may explain several curious aspects of the statute. These 
include the classification of ratemaking as rulemaking, see 5 U.S.C. § 551(4), 
the reference to “particular appficabihty” in the definition of rulemaking, see 
id., and the various exemptions for rulemaking or ratemaking that are found 
within the hearing provisions, see id. §§ 554(d), 556(d), 557(b).
3. 
The Choice Between Adjudication and Rulemaking. Congress often 
authorizes an agency to use both rulemaking and adjudication to implement 
its statute. In SEC v. Chenery Corp., 332 U.S. 194 (1947) (Chenery IT), which 
you win read in Chapter 5, the Supreme Court held that “the choice made 
between proceeding by general rule or by individual, ad hoc litigation is one 
that hes primarily in the informed discretion of the administrative agency.” Id. 
at 203. This is often referred to as the “Chenery IIprinciple.”
2. WHAT CAN AGENCIES 
CONSTITUTIONALLY ADJUDICATE?
Federal executive officers have exercised adjudicatory authority since 
the days of the very first Congress, and state executive officials have been 
at it since even before that. See Richard H. Fallon, Jr., Of Legislative 
Courts, Administrative Agencies, and Article III, 101 Ha r v . L. Re v . 915, 
919 (1988). Yet Article III, § 1 of the Constitution provides:
The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one 
supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may 
from time to time ordain and establish. The Judges, both of the
